alt: Three stages of the entrepreneur’s role: create and set up (spot a gap, test, raise finance), run the business (day-to-day decisions, often harder than start-up) and expand or develop (new products or markets, employ managers and delegate). Below, intrapreneurship: an employee innovating inside an existing firm, which gains innovation while the employee gains freedom with less risk.
caption: The role shifts from creating to running to delegating; intrapreneurs innovate from inside.

alt: Five barriers to entrepreneurship: finance without a track record, lack of experience, regulations, established rivals with brand loyalty and scale, and personal financial risk. Risk is reduced by research, a business plan, starting small and testing; uncertainty cannot be removed, so entrepreneurs keep reserves and flexibility.
caption: Research and planning reduce risk; reserves and flexibility help with uncertainty.

alt: Characteristics (determination and resilience, calculated risk-taking, creativity and initiative, self-confidence) and skills (planning, communication, financial understanding, selling, team building). Each should be linked to a case: resilience matters when early sales disappoint; communication matters when persuading a bank or supplier.
caption: Link a characteristic to the moment in the case when it matters.

alt: Motives split into financial (profit maximisation and profit satisficing) and non-financial (ethical stance, social entrepreneurship, independence and home working). An owner who opens five days instead of seven to protect family time is satisficing, a rational choice.
caption: Not every owner maximises profit: many satisfice or have non-financial aims.

alt: Survival comes first for a new business or one in crisis, then profit maximisation once established. Six other objectives can compete with profit: sales maximisation, market share, cost efficiency, employee welfare, customer satisfaction and social objectives. The choice depends on size and stage, ownership, the market and economy and leaders’ values.
caption: Objectives change with the business’s stage, and most compete with profit.

alt: Amara gives up a $38,000 salary and $1,000 interest (4% on $25,000 savings), an opportunity cost of $39,000. Her studio makes $30,000 in year one, leaving her $9,000 worse off in money terms than staying employed.
caption: Opportunity cost is the next best alternative given up: here $39,000 against $30,000 profit.

alt: Two rectangles show contribution. Now: 200,000 litres × $0.40 ($1.20 − $0.80) = $80,000 a month. After a price cut to $1.10: 240,000 litres × $0.30 = $72,000. Sales rise 20% but contribution falls $8,000 a month.
caption: A wider, flatter rectangle: more litres, less contribution.
